title: It Isn't in Me — Two Years, a Dream, a Granary
blocks: Peace to you, brothers and sisters. Today I want to put a question to you before anything else: suppose that one day the chance you have waited thirteen years for finally arrives — what would the first sentence out of your mouth be?

Genesis chapter 41. A thirty-year-old Hebrew slave is brought up out of a prison, hurried along the whole way; he shaves his head, changes his clothes, and stands in front of the most powerful man in the world of that day.
Pharaoh says, "I have heard it said of you, that when you hear a dream you can interpret it."

Brothers and sisters, all it would take is one sentence — "Yes, I can interpret dreams" — and his whole life turns over. But the first thing Joseph says when he opens his mouth is this: "It isn't in me."
A man who has waited thirteen years, in the single most decisive minute of his life, steps aside first and gets himself out of the way.
1. At the End of Two Full Years
Verse 1: "At the end of two full years, Pharaoh dreamed."
The Hebrew reads מִקֵּץ שְׁנָתַיִם יָמִים, literally "at the fulfilling of two years of days" — the days of two years were full.

That word "fulfilled" matters a great deal. The previous chapter ended like this: "Yet the chief cup bearer didn't remember Joseph, but forgot him." This chapter opens by saying the days were full. With a single word the text rewrites "he was forgotten" into "the time had not yet come."
God's delay is never God's forgetting. It only means that the date has not yet been filled up.

Pharaoh dreams that seven fat cattle come up out of the Nile, and then seven lean and gaunt cattle come up after them and swallow the fat ones; and he dreams again of seven full ears of grain swallowed up by seven ears scorched thin by the east wind.

Both dreams are built entirely out of Egypt's heaviest symbols. The word for "river", הַיְאֹר, is the Nile, which the Egyptians took to be the source of life and of divinity itself; the cow is the image of the Egyptian goddess Hathor; and the east wind — the khamsin — blows in off the desert and can destroy a whole field in a single night.
God speaks to a person in the language that person can understand. He used Egyptian pictures to speak to an Egyptian king.

"In the morning, his spirit was troubled, and he sent and called for all of Egypt's magicians and wise men. Pharaoh told them his dreams, but there was no one who could interpret them to Pharaoh." (Genesis 41:8)
"His spirit was troubled" is וַתִּפָּעֶם רוּחוֹ in the Hebrew, literally "his spirit was beaten about." In Daniel chapter 2, when Nebuchadnezzar has his dream, the text uses this same word.
Not one of the wise men in all Egypt could read it. That is not a coincidence — God arranged a situation in which every single person was helpless, so that one forgotten man would be remembered.
"Then the chief cup bearer spoke to Pharaoh, saying, 'I remember my faults today.'" (Genesis 41:9)
The word "remember" here is מַזְכִּיר — exactly the root Joseph had used two years earlier when he begged him: "make mention of me to Pharaoh."
And look at how he brings Joseph up: "There was with us there a young man, a Hebrew, servant to the captain of the guard." — three belittling words strung together: foreign, young, a slave.
And God used a slighting introduction like that to bring Joseph in before the king.
"Then Pharaoh sent and called Joseph, and they brought him hastily out of the dungeon. He shaved himself, changed his clothing, and came in to Pharaoh." (Genesis 41:14)

"They brought him hastily out of the dungeon" is a Hiphil in the Hebrew — "they made him run out of the pit" — chivvied along the whole way. And the word for "dungeon" is בּוֹר, a pit, the very same word as the pit his brothers threw him into in chapter 37.
Thirteen years earlier he was thrown down into a pit; thirteen years later he is hurried at a run out of another pit.
When God moves to act, two years of silence can end in a single morning.
"At the end of two full years" — is there something particular about that phrase in the Hebrew?

Literally the Hebrew says "the days of two years were fulfilled." The previous chapter ended with "Yet the chief cup bearer didn't remember Joseph, but forgot him"; this chapter opens by saying the days were full — with a single word the text rewrites "he was forgotten" into "it had not yet come." That contrast is the key to the whole chapter: God's delay is never God's forgetting; it is that the date has not yet been filled up. And what deserves even more attention is the speed of what follows. Thirteen years of waiting end in one morning — Pharaoh sends for him, and the Hebrew says "they made him run out of the dungeon", hurried along the whole way. When God moves to act, two years of silence can be cleared away in a single morning.
Why did God speak to Pharaoh through images like the Nile, the cow and the east wind?

Because God speaks to a person in the language that person can understand. The "river" is the Nile, which the Egyptians took to be the source of life and of divinity; the cow is the image of the Egyptian goddess Hathor; the east wind blows in off the desert and can ruin an entire field in a single night. Both dreams are built out of Egypt's heaviest symbols. There is a great deal in this for anyone who wants to share the gospel: speak to a person in his language, with his pictures, about the things he actually cares about. That is not compromise — it is God's own method. We complain very often that other people do not understand us, when the thing that needs adjusting is usually the way we say it, not the other person's ears.
2. A Light from the Original: "It Isn't in Me"
Pharaoh said to him, "I have dreamed a dream, and there is no one who can interpret it. I have heard it said of you, that when you hear a dream you can interpret it." (Genesis 41:15)
Joseph answered, "It isn't in me. God will give Pharaoh an answer of peace." (Genesis 41:16)
"It isn't in me" is a single word in the Hebrew: בִּלְעָדָי (*bil'adai*), meaning "not I", "apart from me."
Brothers and sisters, that one word is far too important to read past. We have to stop and think about the position he was standing in.

He is thirty years old. He has been a sold man for thirteen years. He has only just come up out of a prison. He knows this is his one chance, and very probably his last. And he has exactly one thing in his hand — this gift God gave him.
And the first thing he does is push that one bargaining chip away across the table.

This is not a polite formula; it is the pattern of his whole life. In the prison he said, "Don't interpretations belong to God?" In front of the king he says, "It isn't in me." What he said where nobody could hear is what he says where everybody can.
And what comes of it? In verse 38 Pharaoh says to his servants, "Can we find such a one as this, a man in whom is the Spirit of God?"
This is the first time in the whole Bible that anyone is described in these words — "a man in whom is the Spirit of God." And the one who says it is an Egyptian king who worships the sun god.
Why could a pagan see God on him? Because Joseph kept stepping aside. If you do not step aside, people can only see you; when you step aside, then people can see the One standing behind you.
That is the definition of selflessness: not that I have no share in it, but that I hand my share back first to the One who gave it to me.
There is one more detail here, and it is a beautiful one. In verse 44 Pharaoh says to Joseph, "Without you, no man shall lift up his hand or his foot in all the land of Egypt."
"Without you" is וּבִלְעָדֶיךָ in the Hebrew — the very same word Joseph used back in verse 16 when he said, "It isn't in me."
He said "not I", and God had Pharaoh say "not without you."
Jesus said, "Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted." This chapter acts that sentence out from beginning to end.

Then Joseph interprets the dream: "The dream of Pharaoh is one." Two dreams, one message. The seven cattle are seven years and the seven ears are seven years — after seven years of great plenty come seven years of famine.
Twice he says the same thing: "What God is about to do he has declared to Pharaoh" (41:25); "God has shown Pharaoh what he is about to do" (41:28).
And the word he uses carries the definite article — הָאֱלֹהִים, "the God" — not one god among many, but that One. Standing in a court crowded with deities, he says it perfectly plainly.

"The dream was doubled to Pharaoh, because the thing is established by God, and God will shortly bring it to pass." (Genesis 41:32) "Established" is נָכוֹן, a passive form — "it has already been fixed" — and "will shortly bring it to pass" is a Piel participle. God has already set his hand to it.
"It isn't in me" — doesn't saying that throw the whole opportunity away?

In the Hebrew it is one word, בִּלְעָדָי, meaning "not I", "apart from me." Think about where he was standing: thirty years old, thirteen years a sold man, just out of prison, knowing that this was his one chance and quite possibly his last, and holding exactly one thing — this gift. And the first thing he does is push that single bargaining chip away. And the result? In verse 38 Pharaoh says, "Can we find such a one as this, a man in whom is the Spirit of God?" An Egyptian king who worshipped the sun god could see it. If you do not step aside, people can only see you; when you step aside, then people can see the One behind you. That is the definition of selflessness: not that I have no share in it, but that I hand my share back first to the One who gave it to me.
Is there any connection between Joseph's "not I" and Pharaoh's "without you"?

There is, and it is the same word. In verse 44 Pharaoh says, "Without you, no man shall lift up his hand or his foot in all the land of Egypt", and the Hebrew behind "without you" is precisely the word Joseph used in verse 16 when he said, "It isn't in me." He said "not I", and God had Pharaoh say "not without you." The Lord Jesus said, "Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted", and this chapter acts that sentence out in front of us. One thing has to be said plainly: this is not a technique. If you step aside in order to be lifted up, you are still grabbing. In the prison, where nobody could see him, Joseph was already saying the same sentence.
3. He Did Not Only Interpret the Dream — He Proposed a Plan
A great many people read this chapter and stop at the interpretation of the dream. But the part of it that truly makes me marvel is the paragraph that begins at verse 33.

"Now therefore let Pharaoh look for a discreet and wise man, and set him over the land of Egypt. Let Pharaoh do this, and let him appoint overseers over the land, and take up the fifth part of the land of Egypt's produce in the seven plenteous years. Let them gather all the food of these good years that come, and store grain under the hand of Pharaoh for food in the cities, and let them keep it." (Genesis 41:33–35)

Nobody asked him what should be done. Once the dream was interpreted he could have walked away. Instead he goes straight on and lays out a complete administrative plan of his own: appoint a man over it, appoint officers under him, levy a fifth, and store the grain spread out from city to city.
Brothers and sisters, this is the most practical lesson in the chapter: spiritual insight has to come down into concrete action.
Knowing that a famine is coming is a gift; building the granaries is a responsibility. With only the first, you are a prophecy enthusiast. With both, you are a steward.

Faith has never been sitting still and waiting. Noah believed God would send a flood, so he built an ark — that is the act listed on the roll of faith in Hebrews 11, and the content of that act was decades of carpentry.

And look how detailed the plan is. The grain is not to be gathered into the capital; it is to be stored "for food in the cities." Reserves spread out, supply close to hand. A genuinely spiritual person does things with common sense; being spiritual does not mean floating somewhere above ordinary human life.
And notice the candidate he recommends: "Now therefore let Pharaoh look for a discreet and wise man." He says only "a man." He never says "and that man is me."
"Discreet and wise" is נָבוֹן וְחָכָם in the Hebrew. נָבוֹן is the man who can discern; חָכָם is the man who can carry it out. He sees it, and he can also do it.
And Pharaoh's answer is, "Can we find such a one as this, a man in whom is the Spirit of God?" — Pharaoh answers his own question.
And then, on that same day: the signet ring, the fine linen, the gold chain, the second chariot. "Only in the throne I will be greater than you."

Every one of those things carries a meaning. The signet ring is the ring that stamps the king's seal — full power to act in his name. The fine linen is the dress of Egypt's priests and nobility. The gold chain is the highest decoration Egypt could confer. And the "second chariot" is literally the second chariot — the one that comes immediately after the king's own.

And the Egyptian name Pharaoh gives him, Zaphenath-Paneah, is understood in two ways by the ancient versions: one is "the sustainer of life", the other "the revealer of hidden things." Both meanings are exactly the Joseph of this chapter.
From the prison to the second seat in the kingdom, inside a single day.

And what is the first thing he does in office? Verse 46: "Joseph went out from the presence of Pharaoh, and went throughout all the land of Egypt." He walked the ground himself. He did not first move into the palace and enjoy it; he went out first to look at the land.

Then for seven years he gathers it in, handful upon handful — "Joseph laid up grain as the sand of the sea, very much, until he stopped counting, for it was without number." And "as the sand of the sea" is exactly the phrase God used in his promise to Abraham and to Jacob. The blessing spoken to the fathers lands this time on grain, and it is going to keep a great many people alive.
He could have walked away once the dream was interpreted. Why did he go on and propose a whole plan?

Nobody asked him what should be done, and yet from verse 33 onwards he lays out a complete administrative plan of his own: appoint a man over it, appoint officers, levy a fifth, store the grain spread out through the cities. This is the most practical lesson in the chapter — spiritual insight has to come down into concrete action. Knowing that the famine is coming is a gift; building the granaries is a responsibility. With only the first you are a prophecy enthusiast; with both you are a steward. Noah believed God would send a flood, so he built an ark; the act that stands on the roll of faith consisted of decades of carpentry. Faith has never been sitting still and waiting.
Which details in the plan he proposed are worth learning from?

At least three. First, dispersed storage: the grain is not gathered into the capital, it is stored "for food in the cities" — supply close at hand, risk spread out. A genuinely spiritual person does things with common sense. Second, the description of the candidate: "discreet and wise" is two words in the Hebrew, one of them the man who can discern and the other the man who can carry it out — he sees it and he can do it. Third, he says only "a man"; he never says "and that man is me." Put those three together and you have a model that can be carried straight into today: make the proposal concrete, leave margin inside it, and leave God room to choose the person. And the first thing he did in office says as much again: he did not move into the palace, he went throughout all the land of Egypt and looked at the ground with his own eyes.
There are two more names in this chapter. Joseph gave them himself, and they are his own confession.

"To Joseph were born two sons before the year of famine came, whom Asenath, the daughter of Potiphera priest of On, bore to him. Joseph called the name of the firstborn Manasseh, 'For', he said, 'God has made me forget all my toil, and all my father's house.' The name of the second, he called Ephraim: 'For God has made me fruitful in the land of my affliction.'" (Genesis 41:50–52)
"Manasseh", מְנַשֶּׁה, means "one who makes to forget." And what he says is "God has made me forget" — the Hebrew is the causative stem. He did not forget by himself; God made him forget.

Brothers and sisters, there is something very important here: he is not pretending that those things never happened. He said them out loud — "all my toil, and all my father's house." He put the wound that family gave him into plain, open words.
Only what can be spoken can be forgotten. What is pushed down does not disappear; it ferments.

And let us be honest: this kind of forgetting is not amnesia. In chapter 42 he recognises his brothers the instant he sees them, and he turns aside and weeps. So what this "forgetting" means is simply this: that thing no longer rules me.
"Ephraim", אֶפְרַיִם, means "double fruitfulness." And he says, "God has made me fruitful in the land of my affliction."
Notice it carefully — not "after leaving the place of affliction", but "in the land of my affliction." The Hebrew is בְּאֶרֶץ עָנְיִי, "in the land of my affliction."
Egypt is the place he was sold into. It is the place he was falsely accused. It is the place he sat in prison. And God made him bear fruit there.

Brothers and sisters, this is an enormous comfort to us. You do not have to wait until the circumstances change before you begin to bear fruit. God is able to make you fruitful in the very place where you are suffering — in that office, inside that hard stretch of a marriage, in that hospital room.
And the last sentence of this chapter is the door into the next: "All countries came into Egypt, to Joseph, to buy grain."
In the next chapter his brothers are somewhere in that crowd. That dream of twenty-two years ago, the dream of sheaves bowing down — its time has come.
"God has made me forget all my toil" — can a person really forget?

"Manasseh" means "one who makes to forget", and what he says is "God has made me forget" — the Hebrew is the causative stem, so he did not forget by himself. But this kind of forgetting is not amnesia: in chapter 42 he recognises his brothers the instant he sees them, and he turns aside and weeps. So what the forgetting means is this: that thing no longer rules me. And notice too that he spoke the wound out plainly — "all my toil, and all my father's house." Only what can be spoken can be forgotten; what is pushed down does not disappear, it ferments. The order of forgiveness and of healing is very often to say it clearly first, and only then to hand it over.
5. Distortions You Must Be Able to Spot
This chapter is so well suited to a sermon about turning your life around that it is unusually easy to preach it crooked.

The first distortion is preaching Joseph's promotion as "believe in the Lord and you will get ahead in the world." He spent thirteen years first — in a pit, in Potiphar's house, in a prison. Preach only the ending and what the congregation learns is prosperity theology. The test is this: when the man who is still in prison, whose life has not turned around, has heard you out, is he encouraged — or is he being measured against somebody else?

The second distortion is preaching "It isn't in me" as a piece of polite modesty. That sentence was the pattern of his whole life, and it is the reason Pharaoh recognised the Spirit of God in him. Turn it into a technique of speech and you have made selflessness thin. What the congregation should take away is a kind of life, not an opening line.

The third distortion is preaching the interpretation of the dream and never the storing of the grain. Verses 33 to 36 are a complete administrative plan. Preach the spiritual insight on its own and the congregation walks out with nothing in their hands that they can actually do.

The fourth distortion is skipping over the tension in his marriage to the daughter of an Egyptian priest. The text passes no comment on it — but the names he gave both his sons are Hebrew names, and God is in both of them. That was his confession inside a pagan culture. Skip it, and the brothers and sisters who work in secular settings lose a very practical model.

The fifth distortion is preaching "God has made me forget all my father's house" as "have nothing more to do with your family of origin." From chapter 42 onwards he weeps over that family six times, and in the end he brings the whole household down to Egypt. Forgetting is not cutting off; it is no longer being tied up by it.
6. Two Real Questions from a Chinese Setting

The first question: we are very bad at being praised. Somebody compliments us and our mouth says, "Oh, it was nothing", "It was everybody's work" — while quietly, inside, we take it and keep it. Joseph's "It isn't in me" was not a turn of phrase; that is genuinely how he divided the account in his own heart. Brothers and sisters, this week I am asking you to do one very small exercise: every time you are praised, say to God in your heart first, "It isn't in me", and only then say thank you to the person. Real humility is not denying that you did anything. It is knowing clearly who gave you the ability to do it.

The second question: we are very good at waiting for conditions to improve before we get serious. Wait until the children are a little older, wait until this project is finished, wait until my health picks up, wait until I have changed jobs, wait until I retire — and then we simply go on waiting. Joseph bore fruit in the place where he suffered, and learned how to administer in the place where he was imprisoned. The place you are standing in right now is the place God means you to bear fruit. This week, in the very position you least want to be in, do one constructive thing — you do not have to wait for the circumstances to get better.
Brothers and sisters, let us bring this lesson back to the Three Foundations, the Two Core Values and the Goal of 321.

Jesus is my role model. John the Baptist said, "He must increase, but I must decrease." And the Lord Jesus himself said, "the Son can do nothing of himself, but what he sees the Father doing." My role model is that One — who, existing in the form of God, emptied himself instead. Joseph's "not I" is a shadow cast by that One's "not I."

The Bible is my standard. The standard is not "know how to show yourself off when it is time to compete for something." The standard is "Don't seek revenge yourselves" and "whoever humbles himself will be exalted." Your feelings will say, "if you don't make your case this time you will never get another chance." The standard says that it is God who lifts a person up.

The Holy Spirit is my guide. Joseph did not interpret dreams by technique; he interpreted them because God showed him. Pharaoh said the Spirit of God was in him. We do not interpret dreams today, but we need guidance just as much: when to open our mouths, what plan to put forward, how to lead that household. Rely on our intellect and go it alone, and we end up worried; rely on the heart and lean on the Holy Spirit, and we end up glad.

Let Jesus be King. Thirteen years of training, one layer at a time: over a household, over a prison, over all Egypt. God makes the man first and only then gives him the position. Letting Jesus be King means letting him be Lord in the small things first; the person who will not let him be Lord in the small things will come apart the moment the position gets large.

Let Jesus receive all the glory. "It isn't in me. God will give Pharaoh an answer of peace." Giving God the glory is not adding a word of thanks after the victory; it is settling the account clearly before you have received anything at all.

Establish God's system. He stored up the grain of seven good years, and it saved Egypt, and it saved the whole earth, and in the end it saved his own family. To establish God's system is to build the granaries ahead of a famine that has not yet come — not so that you personally will not go hungry, but for the sake of the people who are still to come.
8. Four Kinds of Heart, One Sentence: "Not I"
We come and stand in front of that king carrying four kinds of heart.

The proud heart says, "This is what I have coming to me." Thirteen years of waiting, and at last one opportunity — who would not want to put himself in the best possible light? Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, writing an ability God gave you onto your own curriculum vitae. Humility is returning to our originally intended position as human beings and saying, "It isn't in me" — and then you discover that the sentence has not made you one bit smaller.

The fearful heart says, "If I hand the credit over, nobody will remember me." Joseph said "not I", and Pharaoh said "not without you." The place you step out of, God will fill himself. It is the place you seized that becomes the burden you have to defend for the rest of your life.

The ashamed heart says, "Someone with a background like mine has no business standing there." When the cup bearer introduced him he used three belittling words: a Hebrew, a young man, a slave. And God used exactly that introduction to bring him in. Your origins are not your ceiling. It is God who lifts a person up.

The wounded heart says, "And what about those thirteen years — who is going to account for them?" God gave him a son's name as the answer — Manasseh, "God has made me forget." Not an instruction to pretend it does not hurt, but God himself handling that pain so that it no longer rules him. This is not something you can do for yourself. Only God can do it, and so you have to hand it over to him to do.
Four kinds of heart, and one sentence for all of them: "Not I." And the person who can actually say that sentence is the one who is genuinely free.
9. This Week, a Few Things You Can Do
First, towards God. Every time you are praised, say to God in your heart first, "It isn't in me", and only then say thank you. Do it for a full seven days.

Second, towards yourself. Take that sentence inside you which says, "God seems to have forgotten me", and change it to, "The time is not yet full." Every time that thought comes, swap in this sentence instead.
Third, towards other people. Take one chance you could have taken for yourself and hand it to somebody else. No explaining, no fishing for the credit — simply let it go.
Fourth, towards daily living. In the place where you are suffering right now, do one constructive thing. Do not wait for the circumstances to improve; do it today.

Fifth, towards your calling. Like a man laying up grain, prepare one thing for the future that you have no use for yet — a savings account, a stretch of training, a successor, a set of notes written down.

Sixth, tell it to one friend outside the church in three sentences. First: there is a man in the Bible who waited thirteen years for his chance. Second: in the very minute the chance arrived, the first thing he said was, "It isn't in me." Third: and the result was that the king said to him, "Without you, nobody in all Egypt lifts a hand or a foot" — and I think the distance between those two sentences is the lesson of a lifetime for me.
Brothers and sisters, let us declare together before God:
I declare that I will step aside, so that people may see the One who stands behind me.
I declare that God has not forgotten me; his day will surely come to the full.
I declare that I will not settle for spiritual sight alone; I will put my hands to building the granary.
I declare that God is able to make me fruitful in the place where I suffer; I will not wait for the circumstances to improve before I bear fruit.
"Fruitful in the land of my affliction" — I am still inside the affliction. How do I use that sentence?

Begin by weighing what that place-name carries: Egypt is where he was sold, where he was falsely accused, where he sat in prison — and the name Ephraim says "God has made me fruitful in the land of my affliction", not "after leaving the land of affliction." The Hebrew is "in the land of my affliction." So you do not have to wait until the circumstances change before you begin to bear fruit. In practice you can ask three questions: in this place, which one thing can I do to the very best of my ability? Whom can I serve regularly? Which capacity can I build here that I will need later on? Bearing fruit is not a feeling; it is something you can actually produce. And if this environment is doing you lasting harm, leaving it is also a legitimate choice.

At the beginning of this chapter, a man is in a pit, forgotten for two years. At the end of this chapter, the whole earth is coming to him to buy grain. And what stands between the two is one sentence:

So the focus is on Jesus — not on myself, not on other people, not on my circumstances. Not I, but Christ. For Joseph came up out of a pit at thirty years old, stood in front of a king and said "not I"; and another man who came out at thirty to begin his ministry said, "the Son can do nothing of himself." Joseph laid up grain and kept many people alive; that other One broke himself open and said, "I am the bread of life."

May God bless every one of us: when we are praised, to remember to settle the account clearly; when we are waiting, to remember that the days are not yet full. May we not only see, but also set our hands to preparing. And may God make us fruitful in the place where we suffer, and bring out of us a double portion of fruit. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

Leader's note: the Three Transformations are one road running downward. The first drives the point of this lesson into the head; the second carries it from the head into the heart; the third carries it from the heart into the ordinary days. If time runs short, cover fewer questions rather than skipping the third — without reaching the third transformation, this lesson stops at an idea.

Priority markers: ★★★ = highest priority; if time is short, discuss at least this one in each transformation. ★★ = second priority. ★ = if time allows. The multiplication assignment marked [Must do] may not be dropped; it can be finished at home.
Transformation One | Internalise — until it becomes mindset (about 20 minutes)
Purpose: through discussion, to drive the point of this lesson into a clear mindset.
1. ★★★ He said "not I", and God had Pharaoh say "not without you." Why is selflessness not a technique?
2. ★★ In the text, "he was forgotten" is rewritten into "the days were not yet full." What does that say to the thing you are waiting for right now?
3. ★ Knowing the famine is coming is a gift; building the granary is a responsibility. Which insight in your hands has not yet turned into an action?
4. ★★ "Fruitful in the land of my affliction" — not after leaving it. How does that sentence change the way you see the situation you are in now?
Leader's reminder: the aim of this section is that people can say it, not that they answer it beautifully. If someone speaks in fragments, help him tidy it up; do not finish his sentence for him.
Transformation Two | Digest — until it becomes life (about 35 minutes · the heart of this lesson)
Purpose: through seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing, to digest the mindset until it becomes life.

5. ★★★ The manuscript named four kinds of heart — proud (the chance is here and I mean to take hold of it), fearful (I am afraid that if I step aside there will be nothing left for me), ashamed (I am still down in the pit), wounded (the person I was waiting for never came). Which are you most like? What experience made you that way?
6. ★★ Read this aloud: "It isn't in me. God will give Pharaoh an answer of peace." Then tell the group: where does that sentence touch you?
7. ★★ What is the "one bargaining chip" in your hand? Which part of it is the hardest to let go of?
8. ★ Finish it in one sentence: "The thing I most want people to see in me is …"

First: there is a man in the Bible who spent thirteen years in prison and went from a jail cell to the second seat in the kingdom inside a single day. Second: the first thing he said when he opened his mouth was not "I can interpret dreams" but "It isn't in me."
